question.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-10,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+15.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
question.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}=3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t))}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{12{csc}^{2}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$
